note: ADR-0011: an ordinary wildcard never consumes the period that starts a component. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule and accepts the candidate; its own frozen Zig filesystem glob excludes it, as path-matcher.jsonl already records. ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.
The same pattern accepts the name once leading periods are opted in.
A literal period in the pattern matches the leading period without any flag.

A single-byte wildcard is bound by the same rule as a star. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule and accepts the candidate; its own frozen Zig filesystem glob excludes it, as path-matcher.jsonl already records. ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.
With the flag the wildcard consumes the period like any other byte.

A character class naming the period is still refused at a component start. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule and accepts the candidate; its own frozen Zig filesystem glob excludes it, as path-matcher.jsonl already records. ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.
The class matches once the leading-period rule is lifted.

ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.

A hidden directory name is protected exactly like a hidden file name. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule and accepts the candidate; its own frozen Zig filesystem glob excludes it, as path-matcher.jsonl already records. ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.

Recursive ** does not bypass the rule for the hidden component it crosses.

An intermediate hidden component blocks the match. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule and accepts the candidate; its own frozen Zig filesystem glob excludes it, as path-matcher.jsonl already records. ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.
The flag admits the intermediate hidden component.
Naming the period explicitly in the first component needs no flag.

The parent-directory name starts with a period and is protected as well. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule and accepts the candidate; its own frozen Zig filesystem glob excludes it, as path-matcher.jsonl already records. ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.

A component-leading star cannot stop without consuming immediately before a leading period. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule and accepts the candidate; ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.
The explicit flag permits the star's zero-width branch before the leading period.

Issue #394: a negation spans matcher text like `*`, which refuses this candidate, so it may cross the separator but not consume the period that starts the next component. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule; ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.
The flag lets the negation consume the hidden component, exactly as it does for `*`.
A negation cannot select a hidden name at depth zero either. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule; ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.
With the flag the negation selects the hidden name.

Issue #394: `a*` refuses this candidate, and so does a negation after the same literal prefix. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule; ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.
The flag lifts the rule for the embedded negation too.

Issue #394: `src/*` refuses this candidate, and so does a negation in the same position. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule; ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.

Naming a hidden exception is not an opt-in: the negation consumes what its alternative rejects, so it stays wildcard-like. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule; ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.

Like `*.env`, a negation may not stop immediately before a component-leading period and hand it to the literal suffix. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule; ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.
A period the pattern writes at the start of its own component names the hidden component explicitly.

Issue #394: the path filter's root negation crosses separators like a root `*` but selects no hidden component. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule; ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.
With the flag the path filter's negation selects the hidden components too.

Issue #394: the embedded negation may cross the separator but not into the hidden component. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule; ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.
The flag admits the hidden component through the embedded negation.

Issue #394: a negation after an explicit separator selects neither a hidden name in its own component nor one it would reach by crossing a separator. zlob 1.6.3's Rust matchPaths entry point applies no leading-period rule; ADR-0011 keeps the POSIX rule as ferralk's primary result.
The component-local reading never lets the negation cross the separator at all.
The filesystem-glob reading refuses the hidden name at depth zero.
With the flag the filesystem-glob reading selects the hidden name.
The embedded negation stays inside its component under the filesystem-glob reading.
The negation after an explicit separator reaches neither the next component nor its hidden name.
A hidden name in the negation's own component is refused without the flag.
With the flag the negation selects the hidden name in its own component.
